### Challenges for new copper mine projects _page 2_ 

In the last few years we have seen serious difficulties on the supply front not just in operating copper mines but also at new operations that have struggled to deliver on schedule.  This article considers the problems faced by new copper projects and seeks to determine those issues that are of most importance.  It will also identify the extent to which these difficulties will continue to persist in future years.  Finally, advances in mining technology for exploration, underground mining and open pit mining are assessed in terms of their potential to yield future benefits and alleviate some of the problems faced by future mining projects. 



 2012 CRU International Limited confidential     www.cruonline.crugroup.com 

<u>www.cruonline.crugroup.com</u> COPPER STUDIES April 2012

##### Introduction 

<mark>The severe delays in commissioning of new copper projects over the past couple of years have been an important factor behind the generally disappointing performance of copper supply.  This article considers the problems faced by new copper projects and seeks to determine those issues that are of most importance and the extent to which these difficulties will continue to persist in future years.  In order to asses the degree to which these difficulties will affect overall copper production, we

also consider advances in mining technology in terms of their potential to help overcome some of the obstacles that are expected to emerge in the future. ##### New copper projects According to our data, 409 new copper projects are expected to come on stream in the period 2012-2022 and their cumulative potential production amounts to 131Mt. However, for most projects the potential production is not always attained due to delays and disruptions. We therefore also calculate the adjusted production from new projects by applying probabilities based on known characteristics and current development status and subsequently applying our standard disruption allowance. The adjusted cumulative production in 2012-2022 is therefore lower and totals 73Mt. As indicated in the chart below, South and Central America is the dominant region in terms of new copper production, accounting for 43% of the total cumulative production in 2012-2022. This is similar to its 42% share of the total annual production in 2011. Asia, North America and Africa command similar shares of new production at around 14-16% of the total. Overall, the ranking of the regions in terms of shares of new production generally reflects their rankings in current production. This indicates that exploration activity is focused on regions that are known to have deposits of copper and are therefore believed to have additional resources. Another reason may be that these regions already have a developed mining industry as well as an appropriate regulatory framework that is conducive to investment in new projects. Indeed, there is some indication that the latter aspect is of great importance. Africa, for instance, has great untapped copper resources but the full potential of copper production has not been realized so far due to the higher perceived risk of operating in this region. Nevertheless, there is some indication that this may be changing with Africa’s production share at similar levels to North America and Asia. Overall, the share of SXEW production will decline over the coming years. This type of operation experienced very high growth rates during the 1960’s-80’s as many operations began leaching copper tailings from older copper mines. In recent times, however, the share of SXEW has been more stable. This is partly due to the fact that there is not much more potential for leaching copper tailings as high grade oxide deposits and mine tailings have already been exploited. Also, smelting capacity has expanded rapidly over the past years and the market for concentrates is fundamentally tighter. This makes it more profitable for miners to market concentrates than refined metal. Another major factor is that copper-gold projects are becoming a growing segment of production and many copper-gold projects are being developed primarily for their gold content. The way to recover both is through concentrating rather than leaching. The disadvantage of the leaching process is that by-products in the ore, such as gold and silver, are not recovered. With the high commodity prices over the latest couple of years, miners are therefore less inclined to develop this type of mine. ###### The most important copper projects over the coming 10 years The table on the next page shows the 30 largest copper projects according to cumulative production in the period 2012-2022, excluding prospects. The subsequent sections will review some of the most important factors that are likely to affect future copper projects and are already causing delays in project development. ###### Project delays In general, project development is at risk from a number of factors. For instance, there may be difficulties securing finance and shortages of skilled labour and equipment. Also, an unfavorable price outlook for copper and its by-products may erode the profitability of project causing it to be put on hold. Our records indicate that the average time from the discovery to start-up is seven years. Larger projects take longer to develop and the typical life cycle of copper projects above 200,000t/y is illustrated in the chart below. In certain instances, project development of large projects may take as much as 25 years from initial discovery to production start-up.  2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES April 2012 5 ###### Mining Project Lifecycle of Large Copper Projects 3 to 10 years 3 to 8 years 1 to 3 years 2 to 4 years
However, actual realization of planned projects is riddled with delays. Greenfield projects are particularly at risk as they usually require greater investment, a longer development period, are subject to a plethora of regulatory barriers and attract greater attention from local communities and pressure groups alike. This is confirmed by our data in the chart below that indicates that the average delay in our project database compared to our 2009 expectations was 40 months for greenfield projects and 10 months for brownfield projects. North America was particularly prone to delays, but all regions expect Europe saw projects move back on average. (Start up dates in Europe were brought forward on average, as more information emerged about Russian projects, allowing us to move these forward.) This is also evident in the chart above that indicates that the average delays in 2010 compared to our expectations in 2009 were significantly higher compared to the subsequent years. The delay to greenfield projects was around 30 months, while brownfield projects were postponed by 10 months. From this, one can argue that economic growth is generally favourable to project development. There also are, however, some less benign effects during boom years due to increased competition from other mining projects and sectors for skilled labour and equipment and generally rising costs of inputs into mining. ###### Infrastructure challenges With South and Central America maintaining its dominant role in copper mine production in the future, questions arise over whether the increased concentration of mining in the region may present problems for the development of future copper projects. In Chile, the mining industry accounts for one fifth of the country’s total energy demand and copper projects in Chile are already facing some problems in securing supplies of water and power. This is particularly worrying since the country accounts for 23% of cumulated adjusted world production from new projects until 2022. These new projects would put additional strain on the infrastructure and additional investments in the power sector are therefore urgently needed to accommodate new copper mines. Indeed, estimates suggest that Chile needs to boost its current power capacity of 17,000MW by 47%, or 8,000MW over the next 8 years in order to keep up with rising demand driven by high growth in the economy. While the government and mining industry are well aware of the need to invest in power capacity, progress has been slow as many new projects have been delayed or even cancelled due to opposition from local communities. Hydroelectric projects have been particularly problematic as most of the proposed projects are located in the Patagonia region and ther

efore have faced fierce resistance from environmentalists. It is estimated that at least 5,000MW of planned power project are delayed or have been scrapped, this includes the 2,750MW HydroAysen hydroelectric project. With looming energy shortages, future copper projects in Chile may face further increases in the costs of power that rose from around US$100/Mwh in 2010 to US$150/Mwh in 2011. Moreover, there is potential for a rise in production disruptions due to power outages that may require investment in costly back-up system.  2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES April 2012 7 Faced with these issues, mining companies are already becoming increasingly involved in the energy sector in Chile. BHP Billiton has recently announced that it is considering building a power station in Northern Chile. Similary, Teck is in talks with contractors to build a power plant in the Atacama desert to supply its Quebrada Blanca mine and Xstrata owns a 49% share of the Energia Austral hydroelectric project. In general, we expect that new copper developments may be required to set up their own power plants and desalination plants which may significantly increase the costs of operations. An additional burden on new projects may be that the expansion of the mining industry will increase demand for important inputs into mine production such as skilled labour, equipment and capital and this is likely to increase the prices of these inputs. ###### Low ore grades pose challenges to future developments One of the main difficulties faced by the copper industry in general is declining ore grades. As illustrated in the chart below, world average ore grades have been declining steadily in recent years, registering a 12% decline over the past 5-years. This is partly due to a decline in ore grades at existing operations as deposits are gradually exhausted and partly due to lower ore grades at new copper mines coming on stream. This decline has been more pronounced in certain regions, with Europe, Australasia and South and Central America experiencing the biggest declines since 2005. Africa is the exception, with average ore grades increasing by 71% over a 5-year period due to an increase in high grade operations in Africa. This result should, however, be interpreted with care as our information on Africa is more limited compared to the other regions. This fact has important implications for long run operating costs at mining operations, as copper ore grades essentially determine how much ore needs to be extracted from the ground to produce a certain amount of copper. Declining ore grades mean that the scale of the mining operations needs to increase proportionately in order to maintain copper production at a constant level and this increases the cost per tonne of copper produced. In the chart below, we have attempted to illustrate the effect of ore grades on costs. Using the CRU Copper cost model we have calculated the net of by-product costs for 6 selected mines, varying the ore grades at each operation and recording the costs per tonne of contained copper. The results indicate that the effect on ore grades varies across operations. The biggest effect on costs were seen at Aitik and Mount Isa. For Mount Isa, this was due to the fact that ore grades play a more important role in underground operations where extracting ore is more difficult and costly.  2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES April 2012 9 ###### Government relations and local opposition to new copper projects Local communities and governments also play an i

mportant role in the development of new copper</mark> projects and may in some instances erect barriers to the advancement of mining projects. 

<mark>Government-related challenges to new mining projects can be motivated by resource nationalism. This term refers to government attempts to secure higher shares of profits from mining.  We have seen a growing trend of resource nationalism over the past few years as the high commodity prices have motivated governments to attempt to secure higher profit shares of mining.  In certain instances, this can also lead to delays in obtaining permits.  In Indonesia, in particular, the government has recent implemented a number of new measures aimed at increasing the government’s share in mining operations in the country. These include regulation limiting foreign ownership in mining operations, renegotiation of contracts with foreign mining companies and implementing a 20% export tax on base metals.  In addition,</mark> the government previously announced a ban on exports of unprocessed metals from 2014. 

<mark>While resource nationalism affects currently operating mines, the effect on projects under development may be much more severe.  Indeed, the result may be a deterioration in the overall investment climate</mark> which makes investors unwilling to commit the large sums necessary to finance the project development. 

<mark>Opposition to projects from governments and local communities can also be related to the potential environmental impact of projects, with delays in permits, general regulatory barriers or more direct measures from the local communities causing delays to projects.  The frequency of this type of delay may increase in the future, as there is some indication that governments in developing countries are becoming increasingly tough on environmental regulations.  For instance, in March, the Zambia Environmental Management Authority (ZEMA) ordered Glencore’s Mopani Copper Mines to shut down its Mufulira heap leaching plant due to pollution violations.  More strict environmental regulation increases the costs of developing and operating mines, which may cause delays to projects.  On the other hand, higher environmental standards in mine operation and development should improve relations with local communities and may help ease the stiff opposition faced by mining projects that has been a cause of very</mark> severe delays in some instances. 

##### Advances in mining technology 

<mark>With future copper projects facing a myriad of challenges in the future, there is a greater need and urgency for advancement in mining technology in order to alleviate some of the problems outlined above. The benefits of new technology for future development can essentially come in the form of reduced costs</mark> or greater ability to extract and process more complex ores. 

<mark>One area where there is great potential for improvements that would have a significant impact on the market, is within exploration tec

hnology.  In particular, new technologies that are able to determine rock mineralization and structure at greater debths could potentially lead to significant additional discoveries. Similarly, improvements in airborne techniques could also allow for exploration of greater and more inaccessible land areas at a lower cost.  This has the potential to drive a very substantial shift in global</mark> copper production. 

<mark>We believe that new and unconventional mining techniques are unlikely to make any significant impact on mine production in the near future.  By significant we mean anything comparable to the impact of the commercialization of the SXEW process during 1960’s-1980’s.  Rather, the general trend in technology development is larger size of equipment, in particular trucks and shovels, and increased automation of</mark> processes. 

 2012 CRU International Limited confidential 

<u>www.cruonline.crugroup.com</u> COPPER STUDIES April 2012 

10 

<mark>In terms of underground mining techniques, further advances in automated and remote controlled drilling techniques can potentially bring some cost reductions in the form of lower labour costs and maintenance costs.  This technology also makes it possible to drill in more inhospitable environments and avoid problems related to heat and dust.  The Sudbury mine in Canada already operates with remotely operated</mark> drilling. 

<mark>Another area with great potential is mechanical excavation.  These systems can potentially replace the traditional drill and blast model with systems consisting of integrated cutting, excavating, removal and rock support operations.  By allowing these operations to be conducted simultaneously, these new systems have the potential to confer sizeable benefits by reducing overall development time and costs.  In particular, in terms of difficult operations such as shaft sinking, often associated with delays, the new technology promises to bring about significant reductions in costs and time.  Implementation and testing of this technology is already underway at the Northparkes copper-gold mine in Australia.  However, we expect that it may take a while to perfect the technology and broader implementation is expected to be</mark> delayed until after 2020. 

<mark>In general, in the coming years we expect to see increased automation of underground mines which requires the technologies mentioned above to operate together and also includes remote controlled or automated loading and haulage and improvements in conveying and crushing systems.  Automation in underground mines is already well advanced and fully automated mines are expected to emerge within a</mark> few years, but wider implementation is only expected around 2030. 

<mark>In terms of open pit mining, the developments mentioned above with regard to automated drilling also apply.  With wider implementation of these technologies we will see reduced costs but no fundamental changes in overall copper production.  O

ne segment that does promise great future benefits are surface mining machines.  These machines have the potential to do away with traditional drill and blast techniques and increase the efficiency of the overall operation as evacuation of the blasting area is avoided.  As a result, there may be significant cost reductions in form of reduced expenditure on explosives and drilling.  Moreover, the implementation of these systems would allow for more precise mining and selection of ores as rock is fragmented into very small pieces.  This characteristic could also potentially eliminate the need for a primary crusher.  However, we expect that this technology will need</mark> some time to be perfected and widespread use is only expected beyond 2020. 

<mark>As with underground mining, the general trend in technology advancement in open pit mining is towards automation.  This includes automated open pit haulage that can bring about a reduction in labor and maintenance and repair costs.  CODELCO is at the forefront of this technology, having already implemented a fully automated haul truck system at the Gabriela Mistral mine. We expect this to become</mark> the norm at open pit operations over the coming years. 

<mark>There is also significant potential for improvements in production stemming from automated crushing and conveying systems with mobile in-pit systems. These can potentially reduce the use of haul trucks and large shovels, thus significantly increasing production rates and reducing operating costs and expenditure. These systems are already operating in some mines and the technology is developed enough to be implemented in others.  We expect to see increased use of these systems over the coming years and it is</mark> somewhat surprising that this has not occurred already. 

<mark>We expect the full automation of open pit mines to take longer than for underground mines, with widespread implementation expected after 2040.  Although the individual advances in technology mentioned above only offer limited and gradual advances in production, we expect that there will be large gains from synergies if these systems are combined.  The whole design of open pit operations may change as new technologies will enable reduced mining of waste.</mark> 

 2012 CRU International Limited confidential 

<u>www.cruonline.crugroup.com</u> COPPER STUDIES April 2012 

11 

<mark>As implementation of new technologies becomes more widespread we expect to see reductions in costs and greater flexibility to operate in more inhospitable environments.  However, this process will only occur gradually over the long term and we do not expect to see any radical technology-driven shifts in</mark> mining over the next 10 years. 

##### Summary of findings 

<mark>We have seen that the development of new copper supply holds increasing challenges as future projects are moving into more remote and risky environments and miners are facing lower ore grades, lack of infrastructure, i

ncreasing costs, less favorable regulatory settings and uncertainties regarding the global economy.  Indeed, we are already seeing that these factors are beginning to affect the process of bringing on new supply as start-up dates for copper projects are continuously being pushed back.  Overcoming these difficulties may require increased scale, larger capital investments and more advanced technology. Advances in mining techniques are expected to gradually bring about some benefits through reduced costs and greater potential to operate in more inhospitable environments.  However, new technology is not expected to bring about sufficient changes in mining operations to the extent of fundamentally</mark> affecting future copper supply. 

<mark>Future developments will be required to abide by strict environmental regulations and invest in infrastructure that in itself will prolong the time required to bring a project to start-up and also increase the overall capital costs.  With greater capital requirements, securing financing for projects may take more time and become increasingly difficult.  Investors may be less inclined to provide funding if they perceive future copper projects to be associated with higher risks as profit margins come under increasing pressure from declining ore grades and rising costs of inputs.  Moreover, the gloomy prospects for the global economy may decrease the availability of financing and have a negative impact on commodity prices which may influence the profitability of future copper projects. Delays to developments may also be caused by technical difficulties as mining operations move to more complex deposits. Overall, we expect that the delays in project development witnessed in recent times will persist in the coming years.</mark>
